title: Asking politely
job: Requests, thanks, apologies in the right register
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE ASPECT OF AN IMPERATIVE is the lesson of this module, and L1 shipped the pairs without ever teaching the choice. The perfective asks for ONE act and is the shape of an ordinary request: Skazhíte, pozháluysta. The imperfective says proceed, keep going, this is how it is done: Govoríte po-rússki. The half an English speaker cannot guess is that a HOST uses the imperfective — Prokhodíte, Sadítes' — and that the perfective in that seat lands as an order rather than an invitation.

RUSSIAN WRITES SENTENCES WITH NO SUBJECT, and a request is where an English speaker meets the shape head-on. Mne núzhno rabótat' is literally "to me [is] necessary to work"; Mózhno vódu? is "[is it] permitted water?". L1-M9's Mne nrávitsya was already this pattern and never said so. Meet it once here: M3's Zdes' net magazína and M8's Mne nuzhná pómoshch' are the same sentence type wearing different words.

A NEGATIVE QUESTION IS MORE POLITE, which is the reverse of English. Vy ne mózhete mne pomóch'? is softer than Vy mózhete mne pomóch'?, because the ne leaves the hearer an unforced way out. An English ear reads "can't you help me?" as doubt or complaint; a Russian ear reads it as the careful version. Nothing about the words explains this — it simply has to be taken on.

REGISTER, decided for the level: vy is this course's default and ty appears in no display until M6, so this module is not an address contrast. What the `formal` chip marks here is the ELABORATED request — Búd'te dobrý, Vy ne mózhete…? — the ones that buy politeness with extra length. Plain vy to a stranger stays `neutral`, because it is the unmarked default of the language and not a tier above it.

The lexical moves. pozháluysta (L1-M3) does two jobs — please, and you're welcome — and Ne za chto is its warmer answer. bol'shóye spasíbo sits above L1-M2's plain spasíbo. izviníte (L1-M10) and prostíte are near-synonyms rather than a clean split: izviníte is the everyday one, prostíte the weightier apology, and both open a request to a stranger.

sentences.cue: Tell me, please, where is the shop?

words.note: The perfective imperative: one act of telling, now. This is the shape of nearly every ordinary request, and its partner govoríte means something else.
The imperfective imperative, and skazhíte's partner. It does not ask for one act — it says carry on, do it this way: Govoríte po-rússki.

sentences.trap: The -te ending is nothing new — dáyte, izviníte and zdrávstvuyte all had it, and it is simply the vy imperative. What is new is the choice of stem, and that choice is the whole module.
sentences.sound: ska-ZHI-tye. The final -te is soft and unstressed, and the whole word runs into pozháluysta, which loses most of its middle: pa-ZHA-lsta.

variations.cue: Tell me, please, where is the table?
variations.changed: a different thing asked after, the frame untouched
the imperfective — not one act, but how to go on

variations.cue: Tell me, where is the shop?
variations.changed: without pozháluysta, and noticeably barer

mistake.why: One act of telling is wanted, so the perfective: Skazhíte, pozháluysta, gde magazín?

sentences.usage: Stopping a stranger in the street. The commonest opening in the language after zdrávstvuyte.
sentences.mnemonic: One act asks with skazhíte; a way of going on asks with govoríte.

words.note: The perfective imperative again, on a different verb. Its infinitive is pomóch', which is what a can-question needs.
The infinitive, and it looks nothing like pomogíte. Russian verbs change their stem far more than English ones, so the two shapes are learnt as a pair.

sentences.trap: pomóch' takes the DATIVE, not the accusative: pomogíte mne, never pomogíte menyá. English "help me" gives no warning of this, and the error survives for years.
sentences.sound: pa-ma-GHI-tye. Both unstressed o's reduce almost to a, which is why the stress mark matters more here than the spelling.

variations.changed: no recipient named — still complete
a question instead of an imperative, and the infinitive with it
a person in the dative rather than a pronoun

mistake.why: pomóch' governs the dative: Pomogíte mne, pozháluysta.

sentences.usage: Anywhere help is needed, from a heavy bag to a form you cannot read.
sentences.mnemonic: Help goes TO someone in Russian: mne, not menyá.

words.note: The vy form of the verb of ability. An infinitive follows it, exactly as in English — the difference is what the ne in front of it does.

sentences.trap: The ne makes this SOFTER, not more doubtful. Translating it as "can't you help me?" imports an English complaint that no Russian hears in it.
sentences.sound: vy nye MO-zhy-tye mnye pa-MOCH. The ne is unstressed and leans onto the verb, so the two run together as one word.

variations.changed: without ne — correct, and a shade more direct

variations.display: Vy ne mózhete mne pomóch', pozháluysta?
variations.script: Вы не можете мне помочь, пожалуйста?
variations.changed: pozháluysta added, softer again
a different infinitive after the same frame

mistake.why: mózhete is followed by an infinitive: Vy ne mózhete mne pomóch'?

sentences.usage: The careful request to a stranger — a shop assistant, an official, someone busy.
sentences.mnemonic: The ne is not doubt. It is room to say no.

words.note: Not a verb and not an adjective agreeing with anyone — a flat word meaning "necessary", with the person in the dative in front of it.

sentences.trap: There is NO subject in this sentence, and nothing is missing. English needs an I to hang the need on; Russian puts the person in the dative and lets the need stand alone.
sentences.sound: mnye NUZH-na. The final o reduces to a, which is why núzhno and the feminine nuzhná are told apart by stress and not by the vowel.

variations.changed: a different infinitive
a different person, still in the dative
a different infinitive

mistake.why: The person goes in the dative, not the nominative: Mne núzhno rabótat'.

sentences.usage: Explaining why you must leave, or why you cannot come.
sentences.mnemonic: Necessity is TO someone, not BY someone.

sentences.cue: May I have some water, please?

words.note: núzhno's twin: a flat word meaning "permitted", with no subject and often no verb at all. Mózhno vódu? is a complete, ordinary sentence.

sentences.trap: vódu is the accusative of vodá — the thing asked for is the object of a verb nobody says. The case survives even when the verb does not.
sentences.sound: MOZH-na VO-du. Both final o's reduce to a, so the two words rhyme in a way the spelling hides.

variations.cue: May I have a coffee, please?
variations.changed: a different thing — and kófe never changes shape
bare, the way it is said among friends

variations.cue: Is it allowed to work here?
variations.changed: permission rather than a request, with an infinitive

mistake.why: The thing asked for is an object: Mózhno vódu, pozháluysta?

sentences.usage: Cafés, tables, doorways — the shortest polite request the language has.
sentences.mnemonic: No subject, no verb, still a sentence.

sentences.cue: Would you be so kind, give me a ticket

words.note: The imperative of the verb "to be", which L1 never needed because the present tense of that verb is simply absent. It exists only in this kind of set phrase.
A short-form adjective, the kind that can only stand as a predicate. M2 opens the long forms; this one arrives early because the phrase is fixed.

sentences.trap: The stress moves off the stem: dóbryy has it on the first syllable, dobrý on the last. Same word, and the mark is the only thing that tells a reader which one is meant.
sentences.sound: BUD'-tye da-BRY. The soft sign after d is audible — the d is palatalized, not followed by a vowel.

variations.cue: Would you be so kind, give me some water
variations.changed: a different thing asked for

variations.cue: Would you be so kind, help me
variations.changed: a different request behind the same opener
the plain version — perfectly polite, simply shorter

mistake.why: The phrase takes the short plural form: Búd'te dobrý.

sentences.usage: Ticket windows, counters, offices — the length is what makes it formal.

words.note: A long adjective in its neuter shape, because spasíbo is neuter. The four nominative cells are here; M2 teaches what they are.

sentences.trap: The ending is chosen by spasíbo, not by the speaker. bol'shóy spasíbo is wrong for the same reason dóbroye den' was in L1-M10 — the describing word agrees with what it describes.
sentences.sound: bal'-SHO-ye spa-SI-ba. The unstressed o of bol'- reduces to a, and the final o of spasíbo does the same.

variations.changed: a different name after the comma
reversed — normal, and slightly warmer

variations.cue: Thank you very much, everything is fine
variations.changed: thanks plus a reassurance

mistake.why: spasíbo is neuter, so the adjective is neuter too: Bol'shóye spasíbo.

sentences.usage: Real thanks, for something that took someone trouble.
sentences.mnemonic: The ending belongs to the noun, not to you.

words.note: A preposition doing the work of "for" here. The whole phrase is fixed — literally "there is nothing to thank for" — and is not built afresh.

sentences.trap: chto is pronounced shto, and here it is unstressed on top of that, so the phrase comes out as one blurred word. Reading it letter by letter will not get you to what people say.
sentences.sound: NYE-za-shta, all three run together with the stress on the first. Nobody says the words separately.

variations.changed: both answers together, which is common
da in front — warmer, waving the thanks away
a different name

mistake.why: The phrase does not take an intensifier: Ne za chto.

sentences.usage: Answering thanks. pozháluysta does the same job and is the neutral one; this is the warmer.
sentences.mnemonic: Three words, one sound, no parts.

words.note: izviníte's near-synonym rather than its opposite number. izviníte is the everyday one; prostíte carries more weight, and both open a request to a stranger.

sentences.trap: Do not look for a clean split between prostíte and izviníte. Speakers use both for both jobs, and a rule that assigns one to apologies and the other to attention-getting will be contradicted within a day.
sentences.sound: pra-STI-tye. The o is unstressed and reduces to a, so the word begins pra- and not pro-.

variations.changed: the everyday near-synonym
the fuller apology, without a reason
the other thing this opener is used for

mistake.why: The vy form is the course's default: Prostíte, ya ne ponimáyu.

sentences.usage: The most useful sentence a beginner has — and it buys another try at being understood.
sentences.mnemonic: Two apologies, no clean line between them.

words.note: The dative of a masculine name: -u on the end. Same word as L1's Iván, in the shape a recipient takes.
The dative of a feminine name: the -a becomes -e. Two genders, two endings, one job.

sentences.trap: mne and vam were dative all along and looked like ordinary words. A NAME shows the case working, because the ending changes in front of you.
sentences.sound: ska-ZHI-tye i-VA-nu. The added -u is unstressed and short, and the stress does not move off the a.

variations.changed: a feminine name, so a different dative ending
a different verb, the same case
two objects — the recipient in the dative, the thing in the accusative

mistake.why: The person told is a recipient, so the dative: Skazhíte Ivánu, pozháluysta.

sentences.usage: Leaving word with someone — at a desk, on a phone, at a door.
sentences.mnemonic: A recipient takes -u if he is masculine, -e if she is feminine.
